name: Case Study Analysis
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Reading a Blockchain Case Study Without Getting Fooled
lesson.summary: A practical checklist, grounded in evidence-based evaluation, for separating a real, evidence-backed blockchain deployment from a press release dressed up as one.
lesson.body:
Case study analysis, as used in this course, means treating a company's claim about its own blockchain project the way you would treat any other claim that needs evidence: as a hypothesis to test, not a fact to repeat. This follows directly from evidence-based evaluation, the general habit of asking what would actually count as proof before accepting a conclusion. Applied to blockchain, that habit turns into a short, concrete checklist you can run on any case study you encounter.

The first question is whether the project is a pilot or a production system. A pilot might run for a few months with a handful of participants and generate an impressive demo, without ever being adopted at real operational scale. Production means the system is actually being used to run part of a real business, day after day, by people who would notice and complain if it stopped working. The second question is who is telling the story. A case study published by the company selling blockchain consulting services, or by a vendor with a stake in the platform's success, has an obvious incentive to describe things favorably. That does not make the claim false, but it means you should look for the same claim from an independent source before trusting it fully. The third question is what the comparison baseline actually was. A statistic like "blockchain cut our reconciliation time by ninety percent" is only meaningful if you know what the old process really looked like; sometimes the honest comparison is against a genuinely broken paper-based system, and sometimes it is against a straw man built to make the new system look good. The fourth, and often the most revealing, question is simply whether the project is still running years later. Longevity is one of the most reliable signals available, because it is very hard to fake and hard to spin. The fifth question, and the one this chapter is really building toward, is whether the application actually needed blockchain's specific properties, a shared ledger among mutually distrusting parties with no common operator, or whether a well-run, permissioned database with proper access controls would have solved the same problem for less money and complexity.

This checklist is what the next several chapters apply, one industry at a time, to real, named projects: supply chains, healthcare, financial services, e-commerce, and retail. Some of those case studies hold up well under this scrutiny. Others do not, and being honest about which is which is more useful, and more respectful of the reader, than repeating success stories uncritically or dismissing the whole technology out of hand.

It helps to keep the blockchain definition itself in view while doing this work. A blockchain's defining features are a distributed ledger maintained by multiple independent participants, transactions linked together cryptographically so that altering history is detectable, and a consensus mechanism that lets participants agree on the shared record without a central authority forcing that agreement. Every case study in the chapters ahead gets evaluated against a simple question: did this specific problem actually require those specific properties, or could a single trusted operator with a good database have done the job just as well?
